The Context: Correcting the Ideological Drift
In November 1951, a discussion was held to assess a draft
textbook on Marxist-Leninist political economy. Reviewing
the proposals, Stalin identified a dangerous ideological drift
among young Soviet economists and "certain comrades."
"They are dazzled by the extraordinary successes of
the Soviet system, and they begin to imagine that
Soviet government can do anything, that nothing is
beyond it, that it can abolish scientific laws and
form new ones.
The resulting 1952 document serves as a strict
theoretical blueprint, asserting that a socialist
economy is an engineered machine governed by
objective laws, not subjective wishes.

Pillar Il: The Paradox of Commodity Production
THE ERROR:
Relying on a rigid reading of Friedrich Engels,
certain pseudo-Marxists demand the Party
abolish commodity production (buying and
selling) immediately upon seizing power.
THE REALITY:
Engels was referring to countries where
capitalism had concentrated both industry and
agriculture. In the USSR, agriculture was divided
among millions of small producers who
could not simply be expropriated.

The Danger of Ignorance: A Case Study
Planners, poorly acquainted with the Law of Value, proposed
fixing the price of a ton of grain at practically the same level
as a ton of cotton (equating grain to baked bread).
The Intervention
The Central Committee was forced to take
matters into its own hands, lowering grain
prices and raising cotton prices based on the
real labor/value dynamics.
The Consequence Avoided
If this proposal had received legal force, we
should have ruined the cotton growers and
found ourselves without cotton.
